summary:
Lens: hosted links, cost and law (section 13). I recomputed the numbers against Railway's live pricing: CPU $0.00000772/vCPU-s (about $20.3/vCPU-month), RAM $0.00000386/GB-s (about $10/GB-month), service egress $0.05/GB, buckets $0.015/GB-month with free egress and free operations, and a combined 1 TB bucket cap on Hobby. The storage and egress rows are internally correct under the research's assumptions (9.6 MB blended clip, 1.12 lifetime factor). The rest of the section has real problems.

Cost problems:
- The Summary totals ($6/$11/$30, abuse under $25) do not match the table ($5/$7/$15-25/$18) or section 19 ($5-25).
- The 100k column cannot happen: the 400 GB global cap trips at about 37k links a month.
- The screener row still uses the old 2 vCPU-s keyframe-only budget, which the plan itself replaced with full-frame decoding. It also ignores the 5-minute long tier.
- The service-egress abuse figure is not a real bound. The Railway origin answers 200 when hit directly, which skips Cloudflare.

Abuse problems:
- The brand band is forgeable, and gameId is client-declared. So anyone can host QR codes, text, gore, drawn sexual content or ROM footage under a kid-safe card.
- The global caps and hide-on-first-report let one person turn links off for every kid, or hide any kid's clip.

COPPA and legal problems:
- The hosted flow builds on accounts that hold children's emails collected without parental consent. That removes the 312.5(c)(7) basis the flow depends on.
- The report form can collect free text and contact details from children.
- The retention list is missing several stored identifiers and the database backups.
- The DMCA and COPPA address rules would publish a home street address next to "Hank's Hits".
- "Send to a phone" is an unplanned, unscreened hosting path.

Evidence sources: live curl checks of hankshits.com and hanks-garage-production.up.railway.app, railway.com/pricing and docs.railway.com/storage-buckets/billing scraped 2026-09-27, eCFR 16 CFR 312 and 37 CFR 201.38, and plan-research-2026-09-27.json research[2].

findings.section: 13.2 Abuse and moderation (screening, per-game hosting policy)
findings.problem: Nothing checks that a clip is really our game. The plan says the brand-band check "proves our compositor made it", but a forger can copy the band. The gameId is sent by the client. The screener only looks for faces, nudity and speech. So an attacker can build an MP4 with the band on it and host other content on hankshits.com/c/<slug> behind a Hank's Hits unfurl card. Examples: QR codes or written URLs pointing off-site (guardrail 4), slurs or phone numbers as frame text, cartoon gore (guardrail 1), drawn sexual content that a photo-trained porn classifier misses, copyrighted video, or Retro Arcade ROM footage labeled as "breakout". The last case gets around the "Retro Arcade hosted off" policy that the plan relies on for Railway's Acceptable Use Policy.
findings.evidence: Plan line 547: "the brand-band check proves our compositor made it". The research spec that this line came from says: "This proves the clip came from our compositor (or from a forger who copied the band)" (plan-research-2026-09-27.json research[2].research.designSpec §6 step 4). gameId is a client field in the grant body (designSpec §5.1 body {gameId,...}). Verifier: "the ROM id is client-declared, so any title can be claimed" (verify.designSpecProblems[17]). The plan has no OCR, QR or text detection (grep of GAMEPLAY_CLIPS.html finds no OCR/QR). The only classifiers named are YuNet, OpenNSFW2 and Silero VAD (line 547).
findings.fix: In 13.2, replace the "proves" sentence with a game-likeness gate. Embed the sampled frames with a small open image model (ONNX, in the same screener) and require a nearest-neighbour similarity to the claimed game's real calibration corpus above a calibrated threshold. The plan already requires this corpus in 13.2 and Phase 7. If a clip falls below the threshold or matches a different game better, HOLD it. This also checks gameId, so the per-game policy (retro-arcade off, apps off) cannot be bypassed. Add two more HOLD signals: QR/barcode detection (OpenCV QRCodeDetector or WeChatQRCode, free and in-process) and scene-text detection outside each game's registered HUD regions (for example the PP-OCR detector as ONNX). Add both to the Phase 7 calibration gate and the forged-set test ("forged uploads" in line 681 must include band-copied non-game video, QR frames and text frames).

findings.problem: Hosted links for signed-in kids are built on accounts that already hold a child's email and name collected without verifiable parental consent. The flow uses the account as an owner credential and shows an account-verified leaderboard score (plus the handle) on the public page. COPPA 312.5(c)(7) lets the plan collect the device cookie and IP without consent only when the operator collects "a persistent identifier and no other personal information". For signed-in children that condition is false. The checklist, which the plan says must be complete before the flag turns on, does not gate on fixing this. Section 19 leaves it as "your call", and the Phase 0 notice only "documents what happens today". A notice is not consent.
findings.evidence: apps/web/src/app/api/auth/signup/route.ts:27-66 takes {name, email, password} with no parent step. 16 CFR 312.5(c)(7) (eCFR, scraped 2026-09-27): "Where an operator collects a persistent identifier and no other personal information...". Plan line 553: "the signed-in account are owner credentials". Line 551: "score shows only when it equals the player's server-side leaderboard best". Line 734 / table row line 709: "#26i (owner decision)". Checklist lines 559-566 contain no #26i item.
findings.fix: Add to 13.3: "[ ] #26i resolved before the hosted flag turns on." Resolving it means signup stops collecting a child's email: username and password only, or a parent email used strictly under 312.5(c)(1) for notice and consent. Existing child emails get deleted or consented. Until that ships, the hosted-link routes must never read the session. That means no handle_snapshot, no acct: quota key, no account ownership, no "My Links" account sync, and no leaderboard-verified score, so the flow runs purely on the (c)(7) device-cookie and IP basis. Open sharing stays ungated. Only signup changes.

findings.section: 1 Summary vs 13.1 cost table vs 19 Open questions
findings.problem: Three different sets of cost numbers appear, and Jack is asked to make the go/no-go call on one of them. The Summary says about $6, $11 and $30 a month and caps abuse under about $25. The table says about $5, $7 and $15-25 with an abuse ceiling of about $18. Section 19 says $5-25. The table's columns add up (0.17+0.02+5≈$5; 1.62+0.21+5≈$7; 16.13+2.10+6≈$24; 6+5+7=$18), so the Summary figures come from somewhere else and are not explained.
findings.evidence: Line 117: "about $6/month at 1,000 links ... about $11/month at 10,000 ... about $30/month at 100,000 ... under about $25/month". Lines 534-541: totals "about $5", "about $7", "about $15-25", "about $18, then auto-pause". Line 731: "They cost about $5-25/month".
findings.fix: Recompute the table with the corrected screener and egress inputs (see the findings below). Then generate the Summary and section 19 sentences from that one table, and state each assumption next to it: blended clip size 9.6 MB, lifetime factor 1.12, 20 views plus 5 unfurls per clip, screener vCPU-s per clip, and RAM held.

findings.problem: The 100k-links column describes a state the plan's own cap prevents. Under the research assumptions, live storage is about 10.75 GB per 1,000 links a month. The 400 GB committed-bytes cap therefore trips at about 37k links a month and pauses new links for every kid. The "$7 at 14 days" option is about 467 GB, which also exceeds 400 GB, and it contradicts the 30-day retention the checklist publishes. The research also warned that 1,075 GB exceeds Railway Hobby's combined 1 TB bucket cap. That cap includes the ROM and Postgres PITR buckets, and past it uploads fail. The plan dropped that warning. Raising the cap to support 100k raises the abuse ceiling by the same amount, so the plan cannot claim both 100k at $15-25 and an $18 abuse ceiling.
findings.evidence: Line 536: "$16.13 (or $7 at 14 days)" in the same row as "$6 (400 GB committed-bytes cap)". Research designSpec §11: "over the Hobby 1 TB cap; fine on Pro; the default live_bytes_cap of 400 GB would bind first". docs.railway.com/storage-buckets/billing: "The Hobby Plan has a combined maximum storage capacity of 1TB. Any uploads that would exceed this limit will fail." Line 560: "links 30 days".
findings.fix: Add a row to the table: "global cap binds at ~37k links/month at 30-day life". Make the cap scale with a reserved-pool design (see the DoS finding) instead of a single fixed 400 GB. State that the 100k column needs a Pro workspace and a cap of at least 1.1 TB, and give the matching abuse ceiling (1.1 TB ≈ $16.50 of storage). Remove the 14-day alternative, or also change the published retention policy to match it.

findings.problem: The screener row still uses the research's 2 vCPU-s per clip. That budget assumed keyframe-only decoding (6-12 keyframes). The plan replaced it with decoding every frame, sampling at 2-4 fps and checking scene changes. The row also ignores the long tier (up to 300 s and 50 MiB, about 10x the work of a standard clip). The 0.45 GB of RAM is an assumption: only YuNet was ever benchmarked, and onnxruntime's arena keeps its peak memory. At the verifier's 2-6 vCPU-s per 30 s clip, 100k links cost about 95k×6 + 5k×60 = 870k vCPU-s ≈ $6.7 of CPU plus $4.5-7 of RAM, so about $11-14 instead of about $6. An attacker using long clips under the 60 GB/day cap gets 1,144 clips a day × 60 vCPU-s × 30 ≈ 2.06M vCPU-s ≈ $16 of CPU. The screener's worst case is then about $20, not about $7, and the total ceiling is about $31, not $18. If the daily caps count only committed bytes, as 13.2 says the global trips do, then rejected uploads are limited only by concurrency. At 2 jobs × 1 vCPU that is about $40.6 a month, and the plan never states that bound.
findings.evidence: Line 547: "every frame is decoded and sampled at 2-4 fps plus scene changes". Research designSpec §6: "Budget 2 vCPU-s per 30 s clip" (keyframe-only, '-skip_frame nokey'). §11: "Screener: 2 vCPU-s per clip; 0.45 GB RAM". verify.designSpecProblems[2]: "Budget roughly 2-6 vCPU-s per 30 s clip". verify.summary: "Only YuNet was benchmarked, so the NSFW and VAD cost figures are extrapolations." Long tier: designSpec §3 "duration <= 300.5 s, video <= 52,428,800 B". railway.com/pricing: CPU $0.00000772/vCPU-s, memory $0.00000386/GB-s.
findings.fix: Add a Phase 7 gate before the flag turns on. Deploy the screener to a Railway staging environment and run at least 200 real standard and long clips through it. Record p50/p95 vCPU-s per clip for each tier and the steady-state RSS from Railway metrics. Rebuild the row from those numbers. Write down the hard bound: fixed concurrency × per-job CPU cap (cgroup or ulimit) × 730 h × $20.3. Count every screened upload, rejected ones included, against the daily caps. Give the long tier its own lower per-identity and global daily quota.

findings.section: 13.1 cost table, service egress abuse cell
findings.problem: "About $5 (per-IP limits)" is a guess, not a bound. Per-IP limits do nothing against distributed traffic. The origin hanks-garage-production.up.railway.app is also publicly reachable, so an attacker can skip Cloudflare's HTML cache and DDoS protection and bill every response to Railway service egress. /c/* runs on the same single web service as all 26 games, so a flood also slows the games. The research spec's Railway soft usage alert is missing from the plan.
findings.evidence: curl -I https://hanks-garage-production.up.railway.app/ on 2026-09-27 returned HTTP/2 200, server: railway-hikari, x-railway-edge: atl1. hankshits.com returns server: cloudflare. Plan line 537: "about $5 (per-IP limits)". Research designSpec §11: "a generous ceiling of 100 GB is $5" (an assumption). designSpec §1: "Railway soft usage alert (email, not a hard limit) at about current run-rate + $25". The plan has no usage-alert item (grep shows none).
findings.fix: Add to 13.1/13.2: (1) An origin lock. A Cloudflare Transform Rule adds a secret header, and middleware rejects requests to /c/* and /api/clips* that do not carry it, or the public railway.app service domain is removed. (2) A global /c/* request and byte breaker in Postgres that serves a tiny 429 or static fallback when over budget and pushes an alert. (3) The Railway soft usage alert, never a hard limit. Then state the real egress bound from the breaker setting.

findings.problem: "They never latch off for everyone" is false under the stated design. Every identity key is nearly free to rotate. Cookies can be dropped, signup is free, and per-IPv6-/64 caps fall to a free routed /48 (65,536 /64s from a tunnel broker). With 17 of those /64s an attacker can use up the global 5,000/day count cap every day. By filling the 400 GB committed-bytes cap with screen-passing content (real gameplay recorded with our own client) and renewing it, they keep new links paused for every kid for 30-90 days. The screener's concurrency of 2 has no fairness rule either. A backlog of long clips pushes kids' clips into the research's screen_timeout → HELD path.
findings.evidence: Line 550: "IPv6 truncated to /64 ... Global trips count only committed bytes ... auto-recover with backoff. They never latch off for everyone." Research designSpec §7: per IP 300/day, device 20/day, global daily_count_cap 5,000, daily_bytes_cap 60 GB, live_bytes_cap 400 GB. §5.5: renew to 90 d. §6: "concurrency 2". §8c: "screening older than 30 min: HELD with reason screen_timeout".
findings.fix: Replace the single global pool with reserved pools. New or unknown identities can use up only their own pool. Established identities (device cookie at least N days old with clean links, or an account at least N days old) get a separate protected pool. Add hierarchical keys: IPv6 /64, /56 and /48, IPv4 /24 with a school-NAT allowance, and ASN from the public-domain iptoasn dataset (no account needed). Add a client proof-of-work on grants from unestablished identities (1-2 s on a phone, no third party). Give unestablished uploads a short default TTL and no renew. Make the screening queue fair per identity, with established identities first, and on timeout retry instead of HOLD. Delete the "never latch off for everyone" sentence unless the tests prove it.

findings.problem: Any anonymous reporter can hide any kid's clip at once by picking "real person", "private info" or "intimate imagery". Reporter reputation is keyed on the same rotatable IP /64, so a bully can hide a classmate's links forever, and each hide lands in Jack's queue. The research sweeper deletes held clips after 7 days if nobody reviews them, and the plan never says what the kid sees then. The "rare held or reported clip" claim has no numbers behind it. The calibration target of zero holds on about 1,300 corpus clips only bounds the false-hold rate at about 0.23% (rule of three), which is about 230 holds a month at 100k links, before counting reports. The verifier's auto-restore fix was dropped.
findings.evidence: Line 548: "hides the clip at once, pending review ... Reports from reporters with a record of overturned reports lose auto-hide power." Line 123: "reviews the rare held or reported clip". Research designSpec §8d: "held older than 7 days without an admin decision: DELETE". §13 gate 3: "at least 50 clips per game across all 26 games ... zero holds on the corpus". verify.designSpecProblems[16]: "Add an auto-restore rule for reports from low-reputation reporters on clips with clean screener scores."
findings.fix: Add the auto-restore rule. A clip whose screener scores are clean, reported by an unestablished reporter, is restored after a set number of hours unless a second independent established reporter agrees or an admin confirms. Intimate-imagery reports stay hidden. Publish a review SLA, name a backup reviewer, and add a hold-and-report volume alarm. Define the kid-facing outcome when a hold expires unreviewed (a toast in My Clips, with the local clip untouched). Never auto-delete nudity holds before a human has looked, because those are the ones that may carry 2258A duties.

findings.problem: "Send to a phone" stores a clip on the server (a 48-hour single-download transfer), so it is a hosted object. Yet section 12 offers it on desktop during the local phases, and section 13 says local sharing needs no server. It has no phase or PR, no cost row, no caps, no retention entry, and no rule that it passes the validator and screener. An unscreened single-download upload on the hankshits.com domain is a ready-made channel for swapping illegal files, and 2258A duties do not stop at unlisted links.
findings.evidence: Lines 506-507 list "Send to a phone (QR)" for desktop and Firefox. Line 514: "short-lived private transfer: single download, 48 hours, no page". Line 521: "Local sharing (Phases 2-6) needs none of it." Line 117: "Everything except hosted links runs on the kid's device, so the server cost is $0." Phases 0-7 (lines 617-682) have no Send-to-a-phone PR. The cost table (534-541) has no row for it.
findings.fix: Define Send to a phone in section 13 as a hosted object type. It goes through the same grant, exact-bytes presign, validator, screener, identity caps and sweeper (48 h). It gets a cost row and a 312.10 retention line, and it ships in Phase 7 behind the hosted flag. Until then, remove it from the section 12 table so the desktop fallback is Save or Download only.

findings.problem: The report flow lets a child type free text and contact details on a child-directed site. The research data model has details text up to 1,000 characters and a reporter_contact field, and the plan keeps report records for 12 months. That is collecting personal information from a child with no COPPA exception to rely on. The one-time-response exception, 312.5(c)(3), requires deleting the data promptly. DMCA and TAKE IT DOWN follow-ups need repeated contact, which that exception does not cover. The plan also does not put the COPPA notice link at the places where information is collected (the Make-a-link sheet and the report form), as 312.4(d) requires.
findings.evidence: Research designSpec §4 clip_reports: "details text <= 1000; reporter_contact text null (DMCA/TIDA only)". Plan line 548: "Reports: no account needed." Line 560: "report records 12 months". 16 CFR 312.4(d): the link must appear "at each area of the website or online service where personal information is collected from children ... in close proximity to the requests". Plan line 621 links the notice only "from the footer and signup".
findings.fix: Make the in-page kid report a set of structured reason chips with no text box and no contact field. Move DMCA and TAKE IT DOWN into separate forms under /legal, labeled for grown-ups or the person shown. Delete contact details once the request is resolved. Keep report records without contact details for 12 months. Add the notice link to the Make-a-link sheet, the report form and the /c/ page footer.

findings.problem: Both registrations publish a mailing address next to a site named after a child. The DMCA directory publishes the service provider's name and physical street address, and alternate names such as "Hank's Hits" must be listed. The COPPA notice must give the operator's address on the site itself, whose footer says "Made for Hank". Done with a home address, that ties a 9-year-old's first name to the family's home, which guardrail 7 exists to prevent. The plan mentions the address only as a fact and gives no safe option.
findings.evidence: 37 CFR 201.38(b)(1)(i)-(ii): "full legal name and physical street address of the service provider". A PO box needs a written waiver, which is free and granted for "a demonstrable threat to an individual's personal safety". 201.38(b)(2): alternate names include website names. 16 CFR 312.4(d)(1): the notice must state the operator's "name, address, telephone number, and email address". apps/web/src/config/site.json: siteName "Hank's Hits", ownerName "Hank". Plan line 562: "publishes a name and street address unless a PO box is approved".
findings.fix: Add to 13.3, before registration: "[ ] File the free PO-box waiver (poboxwaiver@copyright.gov) citing child safety; use a PO box or other non-home mailing address for both the DMCA designation and the /privacy operator address. Never publish a home street address."

findings.problem: The retention list that gates the flag is missing several stored identifiers and records. It omits the stable reputation HMAC key and repeat-infringer strike records (no deletion timeframe, so they are kept indefinitely, which 312.10 forbids), the 1-year hh_did device cookie, the encrypted uploader IP, the 1-year 2258A legal hold, Postgres PITR backups that keep "deleted" rows, and the rule that clips held for a detected face or voice are deleted as soon as that is confirmed. The research checklist had most of these, and the plan dropped them. The required 312.4(d)(3) statement of the specific internal operations for the persistent identifiers is also not listed.
findings.evidence: Plan line 560 lists only "links 30 days ... held clips 7 days, counters 48 hours, report records 12 months". Line 550 adds "a stable reputation key" with no retention. 16 CFR 312.10: "may not be retained indefinitely ... timeframe for deletion". 312.4(d)(3) requires naming "the specific internal operations" for (c)(7) identifiers. Research checklist (designSpec §12) had "held clips deleted within 7 d, or at once if PI is confirmed ... IP ciphertext ... legal hold (1 y) ... DB PITR backups roll off". Memory file: Postgres PITR archives to bucket postgres-pitr-a4nmqurghp0.
findings.fix: Replace line 560 with the full list, each item with a purpose and a deletion time: reputation HMAC and strike records (for example 12 months after the last event), hh_did (1 year), IP ciphertext (deleted with the clip, or 1 year under legal hold), legal hold (1 year), PITR window (days), face/voice holds (deleted on confirmation), and edge caches (5 minutes). Add "[ ] 312.4(d)(3) internal-operations statement for hh_did, the IP and the reputation keys" as its own checklist item.

findings.problem: The research checklist had an Online Safety Act "UK-links" assessment, and the plan dropped it. Hosted clip links are user-generated content that other users can encounter, which makes them a user-to-user service under the OSA, and the OSA has no size exemption. EU DSA notice-and-action (Art. 16) and statement-of-reasons (Art. 17) duties for hosting services were never assessed either.
findings.evidence: Plan line 565: "UK: a short DPIA; no feed, profile, comments...". Research designSpec §12: "[ ] OSA: record the UK-links assessment and revisit if UK traffic becomes significant."
findings.fix: Add "[ ] Record the OSA links-with-UK assessment (and the illegal-content risk assessment if it applies) and a DSA applicability note; re-check when UK or EU traffic passes a stated threshold from the field counters."

findings.problem: The alert payload is never specified. If an alert carries a poster, frame or thumbnail of a clip held for nudity or a face, it sends a child's image to a third party and could transmit apparent CSAM to Jack's phone. Pushover is also missing from the 312.8(c) service-provider assurances.
findings.evidence: Plan line 548: "Admin alerts go to Pushover (already owned)." Line 554: "frames blurred until clicked" covers the console only. Line 561 lists assurances from "Railway and Cloudflare" only.
findings.fix: State in 13.2 that alerts carry only values: clip id, reason code, counts and a console link, and never images or slugs of held content. Add a unit test on the alert payload builder.

findings.problem: The school-filter fallback covers uploads only. If a managed Chromebook's filter blocks *.t3.storageapi.dev, the 302 playback breaks too, and kids at school are a core audience. The only playback fallback, proxying through the service, costs $0.05/GB of service egress, the $112/month at 10k class the plan rejects. There is no cost row or cap for it.
findings.evidence: Line 681: "grey-cloud upload fallback if the bucket domain is blocked". docs.railway.com/storage-buckets/billing: "If your service sends data to users ... that traffic counts as service egress." Line 528: proxying "would cost about $112/month at 10,000 clips".
findings.fix: Extend the Phase 7 managed-Chromebook gate to playback. If playback is blocked, design a capped grey-cloud playback proxy used only after a failed direct load, add its cost row with the cap, and give the kid-visible message when the cap is hit.

findings.problem: The legal checklist exists only as prose. Other kids clone this repo (project CLAUDE.md), so a clone that sets up a bucket could turn on public hosting with no DMCA agent, no NCMEC registration and no moderator.
findings.evidence: CLAUDE.md: "Other kids may clone this too." Plan line 521: "turns on only after the legal checklist below is complete". There is no code-level enforcement.
findings.fix: Make hosted mode fail closed in code. The grant route returns 503 unless explicit attestation env vars are set (DMCA agent registration number, NCMEC ESP id, moderator allowlist non-empty, privacy notice version). Add a test that a fresh clone with only a bucket configured cannot make links.

findings.problem: Section 19 dropped the game-speed decision the research explicitly reserved for Jack. The body calls the half-speed loops a defect to fix, while Appendix A keeps kids at today's half speed. Because of this, the Phase 1 exit gate "right speed" has no definition.
findings.evidence: Sec 1 line 133 gate: "All 26 games play at the right speed on 60/120 Hz". Sec 17 line 688 lists "half speed (dino, endless, blitz-bomber)" as a defect class fixed by PR 1.2. Appendix A (line 946 and the dino entry) says "apply SIM_TIME_SCALE=0.5 ... so the speed is unchanged for kids ... Flag this choice to Jack: 1.0 gives the designed speed". The research groupNotes say "Jack decides whether to restore the designed 1.0; this is a gameplay feel choice, not the spec's". Section 19 has no such question. The platformer spec keeps its half-rate physics ("Fix without changing the tuned movement feel"), yet PR 1.2 says it will migrate every re-creating loop, which would double platformer physics speed unless timeScale 0.5 is also applied.
findings.fix: Add a Section 19 question: "Blitz, Dino, Endless and Platformer physics have run at half the designed speed on every device since launch. Keep today's feel (timeScale 0.5, recommended) or restore 1.0?" Rewrite the Phase 1 gate as a per-game table of target speeds (for example blitz plane 89-90 px/s, dino score 3.0/s, asteroids and breakout per-frame steps at 60 steps/s) and assert each target in the loop tests. If Jack picks 1.0, add a best-score continuity step to PR 1.2, because every stored best was earned at half speed.

findings.problem: The shared useGameLoop runs a fixed 60 Hz step with no render interpolation. On 90 Hz and 144 Hz screens the frame-stepped games (asteroids, breakout) will stutter: an uneven 0/1/1 step pattern at 90 Hz and 0/0/1/0/1 at 144 Hz. They are smooth today, only too fast. The Phase 1 gate tests only 60 Hz and 120 Hz, the two rates where a fixed step shows no judder, so this regression ships live to kids unseen.
findings.evidence: research groupNotes: "useGameLoop(cb, { running, fixedStepMs?, maxDtMs = 50, timeScale }) ... Frame-stepped simulations (asteroids, breakout) use fixedStepMs 1000/60". There is no alpha or interpolation anywhere in the spec (a grep for alpha/interpolat in the games specs finds nothing relevant). Plan 6.2 already concedes judder at "48/50/72/75/100/144/165 Hz" for the capture clock, but not for gameplay. The 90 Hz Android phones and 144 Hz monitors that kids use are exactly the non-multiple rates. The Phase 1 gate at line 133 says "on 60/120 Hz".
findings.fix: Give useGameLoop an interpolation factor. It passes alpha = accumulator/step to render, and frame-stepped games lerp their drawn positions. The alternative is converting their per-frame steps to dt-scaled steps. Add 90 Hz and 144 Hz fake-rAF cases (11.11 ms and 6.94 ms) to the loop tests that assert evenly spaced drawn positions. Add 90 Hz and 144 Hz to the Phase 1 exit gate.

findings.problem: The CLIPS_MODE flag has no mechanism that works with how this app renders and deploys. The phase table also misstates what reaches kids. Four gaps: (1) Every game route is a statically prerendered "use client" page and the root layout is static, so a server read of the variable at build time is frozen into the page. The Dockerfile declares no ARG, so a build-time read sees undefined and a Railway variable flip does nothing. (2) The static iframe preludes (public/emulator/index.html, the srcdoc prepend) cannot see a server env at all. (3) Per-game fixes in Phases 2-4 (Appendix A prerequisite fixes, 2048 slide animation, Wordle reveal, checkers and quoridor AI fixes, Monster Truck physics pause) merge to master and ship live, whatever the flag says. (4) Kid clones have no Railway env, so the code default alone decides whether their local builds show clips, and the plan never states that default. There is also no rollback procedure, and nothing says the flag survives past Phase 6 as a kill switch.
findings.evidence: Sec 16 line 615: "CLIPS_MODE=off|dogfood|on, read server-side, with a dogfood device opt-in" (no mechanism). apps/web/src/app/games/dino-runner/page.tsx:1-9 ("use client" plus dynamic ssr:false). apps/web/src/app/layout.tsx has no dynamic API. Dockerfile:2-23 has no ARG before `RUN pnpm --filter web build`. Railway auto-deploys every master push (memory hanks-hits-prod-url.md), and railway.toml healthchecks only "/". Phase table line 133ff labels Phases 2-4 "Dogfood" while PR 2.3-2.5 carry "per-game fixes from Appendix A".
findings.fix: Specify the mechanism. Add a dynamic `app/api/clips/config/route.ts` (no-store) that reads CLIPS_MODE plus a signed dogfood cookie. ClipProvider fetches it on mount. Clip UI and workers load only through dynamic import() when it returns enabled. Iframe preludes stay inert until the parent posts an enable message. Set the default in code: 'on' when NODE_ENV!=='production', and 'off' in production unless CLIPS_MODE is set. Keep the flag after Phase 6 as the kill switch. Relabel the phase table as "game fixes: live to everyone; clip UI: dogfood". Add a rollback line: Railway redeploy of the previous deployment, then git revert.

findings.problem: PR 1.1 ships live in Phase 1 and moves drum-machine and virtual-pet onto getGameAudio(). The plan unlocks that context only inside GameStartOverlay's Play handler, and these modules have no start card. The research puts the fallback gesture listener in ClipProvider. That component does not exist until Phase 2 and is never mounted for apps (clips:false by default). So after PR 1.1 the plan has no defined unlock path for them, and the claim that virtual-pet "gets the unlock they never had" cannot be built as written.
findings.evidence: Plan line 305: "creates one AudioContext on the first Play tap (unlocked inside GameStartOverlay's handler...)". Research platform.audioBusMigration (6): "The ClipProvider in GameShell also installs a once-only capture-phase pointerdown/keydown listener, for modules with no start card (drawing-app, drum-machine, the retro-arcade launcher)". Plan 4.1: ClipProvider is "Mounted by GameShell when appId is set and metadata clips is not false". Sec 10: "All apps default to clips: false". The memory read-aloud-start-overlay-shipped.md lists "the four toys without a start moment (retro-arcade, drawing, drum machine, virtual pet)". apps/drum-machine/lib/store.ts:114-125 has its own gesture resume today, which the ESLint ban forces out.
findings.fix: In PR 1.1, put the document-level capture-phase pointerdown/touchend/keydown unlock listener in getGameAudio() itself (installed on first import) or in GameShell. It must not live in ClipProvider and must not depend on the flag. Add an iPhone check to the PR 1.1 live smoke: drum-machine and virtual-pet make sound on the first tap.

findings.problem: Phase 1 ships unflagged changes to every game that cost performance, and its exit gate has no frame-time check. PR 1.1 adds a master limiter plus an always-pulled AudioWorklet tap. That is capture plumbing with no consumer until Phase 6, and it runs for every kid on every game. It also adds an iframe shim that calls parent.__hankClipAudio, a Phase 2 API. PR 1.7 raises canvas backing stores to 1.5-2x DPR on most canvas games, which multiplies fill cost on the school Chromebooks and cheap Androids that the governor (Phase 2) is meant to protect.
findings.evidence: PR 1.1 (line 628): "getGameAudio() bus, iframe shim, tap point". Plan 6.3: "The master also feeds the tap worklet through a zero-gain sink so the tap is always pulled." Research: shim "calls parent.__hankClipAudio.attachForeignContext(this, bus)". The arkanoid spec notes "At DPR 3, render :132-154 issues about 1,500 fillRect calls per frame" and puts its perf gate in Phase 2, not Phase 1. The Phase 1 gate (line 133) covers speed, sound, taps and header only.
findings.fix: Keep the tap worklet and the foreign-context attach out of PR 1.1. Attach them lazily when ClipService arms (PR 2.1, behind the flag), and make the shim a pure pass-through with no clip hook until then. Add a Phase 1 exit criterion: p95 frame time on every canvas game before and after PR 1.1 and PR 1.7, on a low-end Android and a Chromebook, with no regression over 10%.

findings.problem: The Jack-dependency list is wrong and understated. It says none of the items block Phases 0-6, but the iPhone spike blocks Phase 2. Several more Jack actions sit on the critical path of every phase and are not listed.
findings.evidence: Line 120: "(none of them block Phases 0-6, the local clip feature)". Line 190: "memo appended to this doc before Phase 2 code starts", and the Phase 0 gate is that memo. Line 671: "Flip CLIPS_MODE=on (a Railway variable write, Jack's grant)", with a dogfood write also needed in Phase 2. PR 0.3: "Jack reviews the wording". Line 594: the live iPhone and Android flows run "After every deploy that touches clips". Line 593: human steps "Before each dogfood-to-release step". Memory read-aloud-start-overlay-shipped.md: "the session's permission classifier blocked gh pr merge, so Jack merges it by hand", which applies to roughly 35 PRs. #25i blocks the PR 3.4 allowlist.
findings.fix: Replace the three bullets with a per-phase table of Jack actions and hours: the Phase 0 iPhone session (blocks Phase 2), CLIPS_MODE dogfood and on writes, privacy wording review, a manual merge per PR, iPhone live smoke per clips deploy, device-matrix human steps per release step, and the #25i and speed decisions. Remove "none of them block Phases 0-6".

findings.problem: The Phase 0 and Phase 6 exit gates need hardware the plan never confirms exists. Section 19 dropped the research's explicit device-inventory question.
findings.evidence: Phase 0 (line 623ff): "run the lab on Jack's iPhone ..., an Android phone, a Chromebook, Windows". Phase 6: "soaks per heavy game on the oldest supported iPhone and a 2-3 GB Android". Line 593: "a school Chromebook ... older iOS if available". The research device-test-infra openQuestions include "Which devices do Hank and his friends actually use ... Who in the household can provide them?" and "May the SM-X230 kiosk tablet ... be taken off dashboard duty". Neither appears in Section 19. No paid device cloud is allowed (guardrail 3).
findings.fix: Add the device inventory to Section 19 (the model and OS of each available iPhone, Android and Chromebook, plus the SM-X230). For each required matrix row, name the device or a fallback that is free and on hand, such as a borrowed family device or the kiosk tablet. If a row has no device, rewrite that gate as "blocked on hardware" instead of leaving a gate nobody can meet.

findings.problem: As written, the Phase 3 exit gate cannot pass. Retro Arcade already crashes on iPhone with no recording involved, from an upstream bug, and the risk register's mitigation contradicts the gate.
findings.evidence: Line 135: Phase 3 gate "Same gates, plus iPhone soak with no memory kill". Risk register: "Retro Arcade already crashes on iPhone (EmulatorJS #1143, iOS 26.1-26.6) with no recording involved | high | ... replay default off on iPhone for Retro Arcade until a soak passes". Issue #28i body: reports on EmulatorJS 4.2.3, the version PR 0.2 pins.
findings.fix: Split the gate. Monster Truck and both Four-Wheelers must pass the iPhone soak. Retro Arcade passes if either (a) the soak passes after the INITIAL_HEAP or no-growth build test from #28i, or (b) it ships with replay off on iPhone, a visible kid-word reason, and #28i left open. State the same exception in the Phase 6 matrix gate.

findings.problem: PR 1.6 stops new syncs of kid-typed names but leaves the names already stored in production. The plan also misses that Four-Wheeler 3D outfit text is the same class: kid-typed and synced to the server, not only a clip-frame leak. Scrubbing those rows is a production write, and it is missing from the grant list.
findings.evidence: apps/web/src/lib/progress-schemas.ts:215-217 (leaderName, party names). apps/web/src/games/four-wheeler-3d/lib/adventureSchema.ts:154-157 (outfit text z.string().max(10), synced). Research dataModel: "47 app_progress rows" in prod. Issue #23i: typed names stored beside an email is COPPA personal info. The plan (line 633) says only "Oregon Trail names local-only (#23i)" and "outfit text to preset words". Sec 1 lists only "the one database migration" as a DB write.
findings.fix: Add to PR 1.6 a reviewed single-transaction UPDATE of app_progress. It strips data->'leaderName' and the party[].name values for oregon-trail, and resets adventure.outfit.text to a preset for four-wheeler-3d. Count affected rows before and after, and read back a sample (the data-integrity rule). Add this write to Jack's grant list. Also note in Section 19 that the preset-only outfit change removes a feature Hank uses today (default "HANK").

findings.problem: The PR boundaries recreate the review-sprawl failure that the carve-out rule exists to prevent. PR 2.1 is the whole engine core, PR 1.1 touches every audio site in 10 modules plus 2 iframe realms, and PR 2.3-2.5 pack about 190 expert hours of per-game work into three PRs.
findings.evidence: Line 639 PR 2.1: "ClipService, capabilities, FramePump, compositor, capture clock, encode worker (video + audio rings, PLL resampler, priming), IO worker (mux, OPFS minimal library), governor, lifecycle, Web Locks". Line 628 PR 1.1 migrates 12 first-party files (grep: drum-machine, virtual-pet, asteroids, 4x four-wheeler-3d, hextris, breakout, space-invaders, monster-truck, bomberman) plus the srcdoc and emulator shims. Appendix A totals 13 Phase 2 canvas games at about 190 h. The risk register relies on "PR boundaries above" as its mitigation.
findings.fix: Split PR 2.1 into at least 4 flagged PRs, each with its own tests: (a) capabilities and probes plus the capture clock, (b) the encode worker with rings, resampler and priming, (c) the IO worker with mux and OPFS, (d) the governor, lifecycle and Web Locks. Split PR 1.1 into the bus plus lint plus unlock, then per-group migrations. Put at most 2-3 games in each PR for 2.3-2.5 and 4.2-4.4, and recount the PR total.

findings.problem: The plan offers "Send to a phone (QR)" as a local-sharing option for desktop, Firefox and Linux, but it needs server-side storage from the hosted-links phase, and no PR builds it. Because of this, the Phase 6 "Full UX spec" cannot be met. If Jack declines hosted links, Firefox and Linux desktop users are left with Save only.
findings.evidence: Lines 506-507: sharing table "Send to a phone (QR), Make a link" for desktop and Firefox/Linux. Line 514: "a short-lived private transfer: single download, 48 hours". Section 19 lists QR "send to a phone" as a benefit of hosted links (Phase 7). No PR in Section 16 mentions it.
findings.fix: Put Send to a phone in a named Phase 7 PR on the same bucket and grant path. Define the Phase 6 share surface without it (and without Make a link). Show those options only when the hosted flag is on. Add a line to Section 19 that declining hosted links also removes Send to a phone.

findings.problem: Section 17 claims pre-existing defects outside this program's code paths are filed as issues. The research's file-as-issue list was never filed. Some items belong in PRs under the carve-out: platformer leaderboard farming is data integrity, and STREAK_ALIASES is a one-line fix. summary:
I found no critical defects in the sequencing lens, but a lot of major ones. The plan has the right shape: a spike first, class fixes, a flagged engine, a local gate, live smoke. It fails in the handoff between phases and in what it claims reaches kids.

1. **Phase 1 changes behavior live with no speed definition and no perf gate.**
   - It dropped the half-speed versus designed-speed decision that the research reserved for Jack.
   - Its fixed 60 Hz step will judder on 90 and 144 Hz screens.
   - It ships an always-pulled clip audio tap plus hi-DPI canvases with no frame-time check.
   - The drum-machine and virtual-pet audio unlock depends on a Phase 2 component that apps never mount.

2. **The CLIPS_MODE flag has no working mechanism.** Every game route is a static client page, and the Dockerfile has no ARG, so a Railway variable flip would do nothing. Per-game fixes in Phases 2-4 also ship live whatever the "Dogfood" label says.

3. **Jack's involvement is misstated.**
   - The iPhone spike blocks Phase 2.
   - Every PR needs a manual merge.
   - Every clips deploy needs an iPhone and Android live smoke.
   - The device matrix (Android, Chromebook, oldest iPhone, a 2-3 GB Android) is never confirmed to exist, and the research's device-inventory question was dropped from Section 19.

4. **Gates and dependencies:**
   - Retro Arcade makes the Phase 3 gate impossible to pass (#28i).
   - Send to a phone depends on the Phase 7 hosted-links work, but no PR builds it.
   - The PR 0.4 lab needs a WASM AAC build and Phase 2 engine code.
   - The header design strands Fullscreen below 340 px while no clapper exists.

5. **PR scope and debt:**
   - PR 2.1 (the whole engine core) and PR 1.1 are oversized.
   - Section 17 falsely claims the research's file-as-issue items were filed; only #18i-#28i exist.
   - The #23i fix leaves kid-typed names and outfit text in the 47 prod rows, with no scrub write listed.

6. **Smaller items:** Next 16.3's automatic AGENTS.md and CLAUDE.md writes, the "same bundle as Railway" claim (Railway builds on Node 20, now end-of-life), migration ordering under auto-deploy, and estimates with no basis for the second 530 hours.

A kid learns a run was great at game over, so a 2-5 minute Hill Climb, Platformer, Monster Truck, Four-Wheeler race or Retro Arcade run is gone except for the 11 s auto-highlight windows (max six per session). Steam's defining feature is Record in Background: a disk-budget timeline you clip after the fact. Medal saves up to 10 minutes. The DOM-replay games already get 'Whole game, sped up'. findings.problem: The shared-device rules assume one kid per device. A guest session's ring is kept when anyone signs in, so a sibling's last 60 s can be clipped under the other kid's gamer tag. The bulk prompt 'Move your 3 guest clips to your shelf?' moves every guest clip on a family iPad, siblings' clips included, into whichever kid signs in first.
findings.evidence: governor 7.1: "keep the ring when a guest signs in (the same kid, saving the run they just played)". storage 8.1: "After sign-in: 'Move your 3 guest clips to your shelf?'"
findings.fix: Keep the guest ring only when sign-in starts from the same run's result screen or pause menu. Otherwise purge it. Make the move prompt a poster grid with per-clip checkboxes and read-aloud, and do not move anything without a tap.

findings.problem: The on-device library is not reachable offline. The service worker's fetch handler is a no-op, so a kid in the car with no signal cannot open My Clips to watch or share clips that are already on the phone. The Home Screen app the plan nudges iPhone kids to install has the same problem.
findings.evidence: apps/web/public/sw.js:12 `self.addEventListener('fetch', () => { // No-op`. summary: "Everything except hosted links runs on the kid's device".
findings.fix: Have sw.js cache the /clips shell, the clip runtime chunks, public/clips/tap.worklet.v1.js and the WASM AAC on first use. My Clips then plays, trims and shares from OPFS offline, and 'Make a link' shows the existing offline copy.

summary: The plan covers all 26 games, and 13 + 4 + 9 in Appendix A adds up. The gaps sit on the axes Jack named. Findings, in order: (1) 'Record their session' is only half met: the 60 s RAM ring plus opt-in Record gives no Steam-style session timeline. (2) The engine caps capture at 30 fps while Appendix A asks for 60 fps and tests for it. (3) The research explicitly left brag surfaces for Jack (leaderboard 'watch the run', a gallery, reactions); section 19 dropped those questions and section 13.3 quietly settled them as 'no'. (4) Excluding all 9 apps leaves Trivia (a leaderboard game with a GameShell appId) contradictory, and it dropped the research's drum-machine and virtual-pet opt-ins without a reason. (5) Clips and the list of live links do not survive a new phone or eviction, and 'durable' is claimed for 30-day links. (6) Desktop and Chromebook kids have no path to a phone until an unscheduled Phase 7 item, and its 'no page, single download' design fails on iPhone. (7) Muted play and the iPhone ringer switch produce silent clips, and the ringer case is untested. (8) Tier V is promised hosted links its own validator rejects, and its shares are mislabeled mp4. (9) The copy deck says 90 days where the policy says 30, and Jack never settled that number. (10) The cost numbers disagree, and the 400 GB cap hides a growth ceiling of about 37k links a month. Minor items: shared-device guest handling, My Clips offline, read-aloud on the hosted page, Retro Arcade on iPhone, and Oregon Trail phase accounting.
